title: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
answer: Mapping financial AI to the rules means connecting each AI system used in finance to the laws, regulations, supervisory expectations and internal policies that apply to it. The work covers credit scoring, fraud detection, anti money laundering, trading, customer service, reporting and other uses where money, markets or financial data are involved. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security because the same system can raise model risk, conduct risk, privacy risk and operational risk at once. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages are one place where this mapping is tracked.

sections.body: Mapping financial AI to the rules means connecting each AI system used in finance to the laws, regulations, supervisory expectations and internal policies that apply to it. The work covers credit scoring, fraud detection, anti money laundering, trading, customer service, reporting and other uses where money, markets or financial data are involved. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security because the same system can raise model risk, conduct risk, privacy risk and operational risk at once. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages are one place where this mapping is tracked.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The mapping runs on a model inventory or AI registry, a policy and control library, and a regulatory rulebook that can be linked to specific obligations. It also depends on data lineage, metadata, audit logs, version history and access controls so that each AI use case can be traced from input data to output decision. Financial data security adds classification, masking, tokenization, encryption, key management and monitoring for unusual access. In practice these pieces often sit across a GRC platform, a data catalog, a document management system and the cloud or on premises environment where the AI system runs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with an inventory of AI use cases and a risk classification that separates low impact tools from those that affect customers, markets or safety. Teams then map each use case to applicable rules, assess gaps, design or adjust controls, and collect evidence such as model cards, validation reports, test results and approval records. Legal, compliance, risk, data governance, engineering and internal audit often review the same mapping from different angles. The mapping is kept current through regulatory change management, periodic testing, incident review and version control, because a model update or a new rule can change the answer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on data provenance, consent, purpose limitation, data subject rights, intellectual property and the terms under which third party models and data are supplied. Provenance matters because a financial AI system may rely on training data, vendor models, open source components and customer records that each carry different permissions and restrictions. Explainability, bias testing, human oversight, record retention and breach notification are common control points, and they often need to be evidenced for regulators and auditors. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which is one signal of how disputes over data, models and automated decisions are accumulating.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more specific rules for AI in finance, more supervisory attention to documentation and testing, and more expectation that firms can explain how a model reaches a decision. AI governance is also converging with data security, third party risk and operational resilience, so mapping work is becoming continuous rather than a one time exercise. Automated compliance mapping, standard model documentation and independent AI audit are likely to grow as the number of AI use cases rises. As the supply of AI tools and vendors expands, the mapping problem becomes larger and more complex.
